analysis.one_liner: Requires states to use independent commissions for congressional redistricting and to hold open primaries.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, committee vote, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would take the drawing of congressional district lines away from elected politicians and hand it to a commission with balanced party membership and no elected officials on it, starting with the districts drawn after the 2020 census. It would also require states to hold open primaries, letting any registered voter pick a ballot in any party's primary. States that refused to adopt the same rules for their own legislative districts and local elections would lose federal election-administration money.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters in states where politicians currently draw their own district lines. Independent commissions tend to produce more competitive districts, which means more general elections where the outcome is not decided in advance, and incumbents must answer to a broader electorate. Open primaries let independent voters, who are shut out of closed primaries in many states, help choose the candidates who will appear on the general election ballot.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters in gerrymandered states, especially independents

how_it_helps.text: Requires each state to draw its congressional districts using a commission whose members are split evenly between the two largest parties and include no elected public officials, removing the power of incumbent politicians to draw their own districts.
Requires open primaries for federal office, so any voter registered for the general election can vote in any party's primary, including presidential primaries and caucuses.
Conditions federal election-administration funds on states applying the same commission and open-primary rules to their own legislative and local elections.

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent members of Congress and state legislators, whose ability to draw safe districts or to win renominations before a narrow primary electorate would shrink. State party organizations would lose control over who may vote in their primaries.

drawbacks.text: The open-primary mandate would force party members to help choose other parties' nominees, which some voters and parties view as interference in private party functions; political parties argue the First Amendment protects their right to restrict participation in their own nominating process, and courts have sometimes agreed.

The financial lever is blunt: a state could lose all federal election-administration funding if its legislative maps or state-level primaries do not match the federal rules, and the bill defines an acceptable commission only by rough party balance and the exclusion of elected officials, not by more detailed competitiveness or fairness criteria.

The redistricting requirement applies retroactively to districts already drawn after the 2020 census, which would force a redraw of current congressional maps mid-decade and create a period of legal and logistical uncertainty for states, election administrators, and sitting members.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and widely demonstrated: states that use independent commissions tend to have more competitive elections and fewer districts whose outcome is settled in advance. The costs fall almost entirely on politicians and party organizations rather than on voters. The main design weaknesses are the blunt funding threat to states and the thin definition of what counts as a nonpartisan commission, which could let poorly designed commissions qualify. On balance, the gains for ordinary voters outweigh the burdens, which fall on officeholders.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced and never moved again; no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote, and the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Brian Fitzpatrick, a Republican, introduced the CLEAN Elections Act on January 9, 2023.
It was referred to the Committee on House Administration and the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
One Democrat cosponsored the bill, but no further action was ever taken on it.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and all bills not enacted died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress and state politicians who draw district lines kept their current power, since the bill died without ever reaching a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows almost no partisan signal: one Republican sponsor, one Democratic cosponsor, and no votes, so the split that killed it was never measured.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and state legislators
industries.note: The bill would strip politicians of the power to draw their own district lines and force primaries open to all voters, making renomination and reelection less secure. Because safe districts are what protect most incumbents, their interest runs directly against the bill's purpose.

Open primaries would end party control over who participates in nominations, and balanced commissions would remove the partisan advantage parties gain from gerrymandered maps. Parties typically resist losing gatekeeping power over their own nominees.
